title: Standardized translaminar spinal tethering to prevent proximal junctional kyphosis in adult spinal deformity correction surgery
condition_or_topic: Prevention of proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) after thoraco-lumbar deformity correction for adult spinal deformity (ASD).
clinical_background: Operative treatment of ASD commonly involves instrumented fusion, but long constructs place greater mechanical demands on adjacent segments and have reported overall complication rates up to 55%. PJK is a radiographic complication with reported incidence up to 61.7%; advanced age, high body mass index, and poor bone quality are identified risk factors. PJK may progress to proximal junctional failure (PJF) or require surgery. Proximal semi-rigid tethering may distribute loads more gradually, but approaches are not standardized and clinical evidence remains limited.
objectives: Assess whether standardized proximal translaminar tethering at UIV+1 and UIV+2 reduces PJK after thoraco-lumbar deformity correction for ASD.
Assess whether the tethering approach reduces the need for revision surgery.
clinical_question: In adults undergoing thoraco-lumbar deformity correction for ASD (Patient), does standardized proximal translaminar tethering at UIV+1 and UIV+2 (Intervention), compared with no tethering (Comparator), reduce PJK and the need for revision surgery (Outcomes)?
interpretation: In this cohort, tethering at UIV+1 and UIV+2 was associated with less PJK beyond 3 months, but not within the first 3 months. Kaplan–Meier analysis indicated a higher probability of remaining free of PJK with tethering (p=0.027). Body mass index was the only significant independent predictor in the multivariable analysis (OR=1.23, CI95% 1.04–1.46; p=0.02). Although the Cox model suggested a lower cumulative PJK risk with tethering, that association was not statistically significant (HR=0.33, 95%CI 0.08–1.31; p=0.11). Revision surgery was less frequent in tethered patients, but the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.289). The authors suggest that early PJK may be influenced by pre-existing patient or alignment factors that tethering does not address, whereas tethering may help moderate the gradual mechanical loading associated with later PJK.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Rodriguez-Fontan et al. reported a pattern consistent with a protective effect emerging over time after UIV+1 stabilisation, while Buell et al. found no significant reduction in PJK at 3 months but significantly lower rates at 6 months. The study’s overall surgical PJK incidence of 8.5% was comparable to the 6.7% reported in a meta-analysis by Luo et al. Its lower, nonsignificant revision rate with tethering was also consistent with findings attributed to Buell et al. The authors note that prior literature places most PJK early after surgery: in a study by Yagi et al. with a minimum of 5-year follow-up, 76% of PJK occurred within the first 12 weeks, and no patient developed PJK after 5 years.
clinical_implications: PJK can adversely affect health-related quality of life and satisfaction after surgery; additional treatment or revision can add to patients’ recovery, financial burden and emotional stress.

The observed later reduction in radiographic PJK and higher PJK-free probability suggest that standardized translaminar tethering may help limit this complication, although its effect on revision surgery remains uncertain.
Because PJK has multiple contributing factors, the authors indicate that prevention may require an individualized, holistic approach.
practice_implications: When applying the translaminar technique, preserve sufficient bone around the drill holes to reduce the risk of tether cutout or pull-through; avoid holes that are oversized or positioned asymmetrically.
Place the tether symmetrically and anchor it securely between UIV and UIV–1 to support balanced load distribution.
limitations: The study had a retrospective design.
The tethered group contained only 25 patients, potentially limiting assessment of an outcome as complex as PJK.
Follow-up was relatively short, with average later follow-up ranging between 35–37 weeks, limiting assessment of long-term outcomes.

The relationship between radiographic PJK, patient symptoms and clinical outcomes was not assessed; revision surgery served only as an indirect indicator of findings severe enough to require intervention.
strengths: No other surgical PJK-prevention techniques were used that might have confounded the outcomes.
The groups were comparable in baseline characteristics, surgical data, sagittal radiographic measurements before and after surgery, and extent of correction.
open_questions: Whether translaminar tethering reduces revision surgery attributable to PJK remains unclear.
The relationship between radiographic PJK and clinical outcomes, including quality of life and symptom severity, remains to be established.
The factors distinguishing early from late PJK, and the longer-term effects of tethering, require clarification.
future_directions: Conduct larger prospective studies with longer observation to assess the course of PJK and its effect on clinical outcomes over time.
Investigate how radiographic PJK relates to symptoms and quality-of-life outcomes.
Clarify the influences on early and late PJK to inform a more individualized approach.
study_design: Retrospective cohort study at the Department of Neurosurgery, Charité - University Hospital Berlin. Consecutive patients who underwent surgery between October 2019 and August 2023 were compared according to whether proximal translaminar tethering was used.

population.description: Adults with spinal deformity who underwent thoraco-lumbar deformity correction. Of 71 patients identified, 59 (83%) met the study criteria and completed at least 3 months of follow-up; 25 received tethering and 34 did not.
inclusion_criteria: Adult patient undergoing thoraco-lumbar deformity correction involving more than 6 motion segments, with or without proximal tethering at UIV+1 and UIV+2.
Available preoperative, early postoperative (≤3 months), and late postoperative (>3 months) whole-spine standing lateral radiographs.
population.care_setting: Department of Neurosurgery, Charité - University Hospital Berlin, Berlin, Germany.

interventions: Standardized proximal translaminar tethering at UIV+1 and UIV+2 using one polyester tether and two rod connectors (Translace™, Medtronic Sofamor Danek). The tether passed through perforations at UIV+1 and UIV+2 and returned through UIV+1 in a figure-of-eight loop; connectors secured it to the rod between UIV and UIV-1. Tension was applied manually to provide balanced force on both sides.
comparators: Thoraco-lumbar deformity correction without proximal tethering.

primary: Postoperative proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK), assessed using the proximal junctional angle (PJA) between the inferior endplate of UIV and the superior endplate of UIV+2. PJK required a PJA of at least 10° and an increase of at least 10° relative to the preoperative measurement; rates were assessed at early and late follow-up.
secondary: Time to PJK and probability of remaining free of PJK.

Preoperative and postoperative sagittal vertical axis (SVA), pelvic tilt (PT), pelvic incidence (PI), lumbar lordosis (LL), PI-LL mismatch, and thoracic kyphosis (TK), including the amount of SVA and LL correction.

statistical_methods: Continuous variables were summarized as means with standard deviations and categorical variables as frequencies. Pearson’s Chi square, Fischer’s exact test, and independent t-tests were used for between-group comparisons as appropriate. Odds ratios (ORs) came from 2×2 contingency tables. Kaplan–Meier analysis assessed time-dependent PJK; stepwise binary logistic regression examined factors associated with PJK, with model fit assessed using the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test. A Cox proportional hazard model evaluated covariates in relation to time to PJK. Analyses used SPSS (Inc. Version 20.0, IBM Corp., NY, SA), with significance set at p<0.05. One experienced examiner, blinded to tethering status, performed all radiographic measurements concerning PJK.
follow_up: Minimum 3 months; mean: 7.8 months, range: 3–48 months. Radiographs were assessed preoperatively, early postoperatively (≤3 months), and late postoperatively (>3 months). Early radiographic follow-up was 16.2±5.2 weeks for tethered patients and 14.3±3.1 weeks for non-tethered patients; late follow-up was 37.2±44.7 weeks and 35.8±41.9 weeks, respectively.

secondary_results: Revision surgery for PJK was required in 4/34 (11.8%) non-tethered patients and 1/25 (4%) tethered patients; the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.289).
The postoperative change in PJA was 5.97±11.04° in non-tethered patients and 2.26±9.7° in tethered patients (p=0.088).

Among 71 patients identified between October 2019 and August 2023, 59 (83%) met the inclusion criteria and had at least 3 months of follow-up. Mean follow-up was 7.8 months (range: 3–48 months); mean age was 70.2 years, and 55.9% were female. The groups comprised 34 non-tethered and 25 tethered patients.

Radiographic follow-up duration did not differ significantly: early follow-up was 16.2±5.2 weeks for tethered patients and 14.3±3.1 weeks for non-tethered patients (p=0.128); late follow-up was 37.2±44.7 weeks and 35.8±41.9 weeks, respectively (p=0.90).
Age at surgery was 70.44±9.19 years in the non-tethered group and 69.92±11.01 years in the tethered group (p=0.424). Female/male counts were 15/19 and 11/14, respectively (p=0.992).

Body mass index was 27.64±5.59 kg/m2 in non-tethered patients and 28.78±7.39 kg/m2 in tethered patients (p=0.248). The number of instrumented vertebrae was 10.17±3.31 and 10.56±2.52, respectively (p=0.307).
Pelvic fixation yes/no counts were 33/1 in the non-tethered group and 24/1 in the tethered group (p=0.158). Corresponding 3-column osteotomy yes/no counts were 31/3 and 23/2 (p=0.91).
Preoperative sagittal vertical axis was 8.62±5.7 cm in non-tethered patients and 10.14±3.27 cm in tethered patients (p=0.119); pelvic tilt was 27.33±8.15° and 23.82±8.89°, respectively (p=0.064).
Preoperative pelvic incidence was 68.81±11.72° in non-tethered patients and 63.2±14.5° in tethered patients (p=0.12); lumbar lordosis was 27.9±12.63° and 28.6±14.84°, respectively (p=0.186).
Preoperative PI-LL mismatch was 40.9±15.36° in non-tethered patients and 34.6±20.44° in tethered patients (p=0.101); thoracic kyphosis was 37.67±17.14° and 34.44±19.55°, respectively (p=0.256).
Postoperative sagittal vertical axis was 4.26±2.42 cm in non-tethered patients and 4.93±2.39 cm in tethered patients (p=0.147); pelvic tilt was 25.68±8.82° and 23.76±7.1°, respectively (p=0.361).
Postoperative pelvic incidence was 67.66±12.92° in non-tethered patients and 63.36±15.27° in tethered patients (p=0.131); lumbar lordosis was 43.65±14.18° and 47.16±10.19°, respectively (p=0.138).
Postoperative PI-LL mismatch was 23.3±17.62° in non-tethered patients and 16.2±17.07° in tethered patients (p=0.062); thoracic kyphosis was 39.16±15.89° and 44.24±16.41°, respectively (p=0.122).

The amount of sagittal vertical axis correction was 4.36±5.38 cm in non-tethered patients and 5.2±3.46 cm in tethered patients (p=0.234). Lumbar lordosis correction was 15.28±13.53° and 18.56±15.75°, respectively (p=0.203).
In the multivariable logistic analysis of PJK beyond 3 months, age at surgery had OR 0.94 (95% CI 0.87–1.02; P 0.13), and female gender had OR 1.75 (95% CI 0.41–7.52; P 0.45).

In the same logistic analysis, the number of instrumented vertebrae had OR 1.11 (95% CI 0.89–1.37; P 0.35), pelvic fixation had OR 0.65 (95% CI 0.03–15.59; P 0.79), and 3-column osteotomy had OR 1.82 (95% CI 0.24–13.56; P 0.56).
In the same logistic analysis, use of polyester tether had OR 0.18 (95% CI 0.02–1.32; P 0.09), and preoperative sagittal vertical axis had OR 0.95 (95% CI 0.81–1.12; P 0.52).

In the same logistic analysis, the amount of sagittal vertical axis correction had OR 0.95 (95% CI 0.93–1.02; P 0.29), and the amount of lumbar lordosis correction had OR 1.06 (95% CI 0.99–1.14; P 0.08). The authors reported that the regression model did not differ significantly from the null model (p=0.06).

In the Cox analysis of PJK development, age at surgery had HR 0.97 (95% CI 0.92–1.03; P 0.3), female gender had HR 1.17 (95% CI 0.4–3.41; P 0.78), and body mass index had HR 1.03 (95% CI 0.96–1.09; P 0.42).

In the same Cox analysis, the number of instrumented vertebrae had HR 0.99 (95% CI 0.84–1.17; P 0.91), pelvic fixation had HR 1.09 (95% CI 0.13–9.37; P 0.94), and 3-column osteotomy had HR 1.31 (95% CI 0.31–5.44; P 0.72).

In the same Cox analysis, preoperative sagittal vertical axis had HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.89–1.12; P 0.99). For the amount of correction, sagittal vertical axis had HR 0.99 (95% CI 0.96–1.03; P 0.72), and lumbar lordosis had HR 1.04 (95% CI 0.99–1.08; P 0.09).

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that polyester tethering at UIV+1 and UIV+2 reduced PJK incidence and increased the probability of remaining free of PJK after thoraco-lumbar deformity correction. Its association with revision surgery for PJK remains uncertain, and prospective long-term follow-up is needed.
narrative_summary:
This retrospective cohort study examined whether a standardized translaminar polyester tether placed at UIV+1 and UIV+2 was associated with less PJK after thoraco-lumbar correction for adult spinal deformity. It included 59 patients: 25 received tethering and 34 did not. Radiographs were assessed before surgery, at early follow-up (≤3 months), and at late follow-up (>3 months). Baseline characteristics, surgical data, sagittal alignment measures, and the degree of correction were comparable between groups.

Across follow-up, 18 patients (30.5%) developed PJK. Within the first 3 months, PJK occurred in 3/25 (12%) tethered patients and 7/34 (20.5%) non-tethered patients, without a significant difference (p=0.384). At late follow-up, the respective rates were 4/25 (16%) and 14/34 (41.1%; p=0.037); non-tethered patients were 3.67 times more likely to develop PJK (95%CI=1.03–13.07). Kaplan–Meier analysis also indicated a significant difference in PJK-free probability favoring tethering (p=0.027), whereas the adjusted Cox association was not significant (HR=0.33, 95%CI 0.08–1.31; p=0.11). Body mass index was the only significant independent predictor in the logistic model (OR=1.23, CI95% 1.04–1.46; p=0.02). Revision for PJK occurred in 1/25 (4%) tethered and 4/34 (11.8%) non-tethered patients (p=0.289). The authors note that the retrospective design, limited tethered sample, short follow-up, and lack of direct assessment of symptoms and clinical outcomes leave the effect on revision and longer-term outcomes uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Purpose: The study assessed whether standardized proximal translaminar tethering at UIV+1 and UIV+2 lowers proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) and revision surgery after thoraco-lumbar correction for adult spinal deformity (ASD). Methods: This retrospective cohort included 59 adults operated on between October 2019 and August 2023, classified as tethered (T) or non-tethered (NT). Radiographs were assessed before surgery, early after surgery (≤3 months), and later (>3 months). PJK required a proximal junctional angle (PJA) ≥10° and an increase of ≥10° over its preoperative value. Results: PJK developed in 18 patients (30.5%). Within the first 3 months, rates did not differ significantly between T (12%) and NT (20.5%; p=0.384). At late follow-up, PJK was significantly more frequent in NT (41.1%) than T (16%; p=0.037); NT patients were 3.67 times more likely to develop PJK (95% CI=1.03–13.07). Kaplan–Meier analysis showed significantly less time-dependent PJK development with tethering (p=0.027). Revision surgery was needed in 11.8% of NT patients and 4% of T patients (p=0.289). Conclusion: Proximal translaminar tethering reduced PJK after thoraco-lumbar deformity correction, but its effect on revision for PJK remains uncertain. Longer-term prospective studies are needed.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Treatment of ASD is increasingly relevant as the global population ages; nearly two-thirds of patients over the age of 59 are affected [1]. Instrumented fusion with deformity correction is currently the principal operative approach. Multisegment instrumentation remains challenging because of biomechanical demands and overall complication rates up to 55% [2]. Adjacent segment degeneration is a frequent postoperative complication: fixed segments can increase loading above the construct, accelerating degeneration and potentially worsening radiographic and clinical status [3]. PJK is a common radiographic manifestation, with reported incidence up to 61.7% [4]. Its risk factors include advanced age, high body mass index, and low bone quality [5]. PJK can progress to proximal junctional failure (PJF), defined by fracture of UIV or UIV+1, posterior osseo-ligamentous disruption, instrumentation pullout at UIV, or symptomatic PJK requiring surgery [3]. Techniques intended to distribute load more evenly across proximal segments have been proposed. Proximal semi-rigid tethering has yielded promising biomechanical and clinical findings, but approaches are not standardized or widely adopted, and supporting clinical evidence remains limited [6]. This study therefore assessed standardized proximal translaminar tethering and subsequent PJK in patients undergoing thoraco-lumbar ASD correction.

document_sections.heading: Design and patient selection
document_sections.content: The authors conducted a retrospective cohort study approved by the Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin ethics committee (EA2/09/13). Consent was not required because the study used retrospective data from routine care. After the technique was introduced in October 2019, consecutive adults with spinal deformity who underwent thoraco-lumbar correction involving more than 6 motion segments were identified. Surgery could include or omit proximal tethering of UIV+1 and UIV+2. Eligibility required preoperative, early postoperative (≤3 months), and late postoperative (>3 months) standing whole-spine lateral radiographs.

document_sections.heading: Radiographic measurements
document_sections.content: PJA was measured as the sagittal Cobb angle between the inferior endplate of UIV and the superior endplate of UIV+2. The methods cite Glattes et al. for an increase of more than 10° over the preoperative PJA [7]; the figure caption specifies that an abnormal postoperative PJK assessment requires both PJA of at least 10° and an increase of 10° or more. Sagittal vertical axis (SVA), pelvic tilt (PT), pelvic incidence (PI), lumbar lordosis (LL), PI-LL mismatch, and thoracic kyphosis (TK) were evaluated before and after surgery. One experienced examiner, unaware of tether-group assignment, performed all PJK radiographic measurements. Illustrative preoperative and 3-month postoperative PJA measurements were 3.12° and 4.56° in a patient without postoperative PJK, and 1.54° and 27.41° in a patient who developed PJK after correction.

document_sections.heading: Tethering technique
document_sections.content: Every tether was placed by the same approach, linking UIV+1 and UIV+2 to the instrumentation rod between UIV and UIV-1. Each patient received one tether and two rod connectors (Translace™, Medtronic Sofamor Danek, Menphis, TN, USA). A 2 mm high-speed diamond burr created translaminar holes in the spinous processes of UIV+1 and UIV+2. The polyester tether was attached to a suture (1–0 Vicryl Polyglactin 910, Ethicon, USA), passed through UIV+1 and UIV+2, and returned through UIV+1 to form a figure-of-eight loop. The tether then passed through connectors fixed near the proximal rod end between UIV and UIV-1. Tension was applied manually with a torque instrument, aiming for equal force on both sides without excessive loading.

document_sections.heading: Statistical analysis
document_sections.content: Continuous variables were summarized with means and standard deviations; categorical variables were reported as frequencies. Pearson’s Chi square, Fischer’s exact test, and independent t-tests were used as appropriate to compare baseline characteristics, PJK and revision rates, radiographic follow-up duration, and time-to-PJK. Odds ratios (ORs) came from 2×2 contingency tables. Kaplan–Meier analysis compared time-dependent PJK outcomes. Binary logistic regression examined independent variables associated with PJK, with model fit evaluated using the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test [8]. A Cox proportional hazard model assessed covariate effects on survival time. Analyses used SPSS (Inc. Version 20.0, IBM Corp., NY, SA), with significance set at p<0.05.

document_sections.heading: Patient demographics
document_sections.content: Between October 2019 and August 2023, 59 out of 71 patients (83%) met inclusion criteria and had at least 3-month follow-up. Mean follow-up was 7.8 months (range: 3–48 months), mean age was 70.2 years, and 55.9% were female. The cohort comprised 25 tethered (T) and 34 non-tethered (NT) patients. The groups were comparable in demographics, instrumentation length, pelvic fixation, and 3-column osteotomy. Table 1 presents group-specific demographic and surgical measurements.

document_sections.heading: Sagittal plane radiographic parameters
document_sections.content: No significant between-group differences were found in preoperative or postoperative sagittal radiographic parameters. Achieved SVA and LL correction and postoperative changes in those measures were also comparable. Table 2 presents the measurements and between-group comparisons.

document_sections.heading: PJK development and revision surgery
document_sections.content: All patients had an early assessment at 3 months, whereas follow-up beyond that point varied considerably. Time-to-PJK was therefore assessed using early (3-month) and late (>3-month) PJK rates. Radiographic follow-up duration did not differ between T and NT: early follow-up was 16.2±5.2 weeks and 14.3±3.1 weeks, respectively (p=0.128), and late follow-up was 37.2±44.7 weeks and 35.8±41.9 weeks, respectively (p=0.90). Across 59 patients, 18 (30.5%) developed PJK; 10 (55.5%) of those cases arose within the first 3 months. Early PJK did not differ significantly between T (3/25; 12%) and NT (7/34; 20.5%; p=0.384). At late follow-up, NT had significantly more PJK (14/34; 41.1%) than T (4/25; 16%; p=0.037). Overall, NT patients were 3.67 times more likely to develop PJK (95%CI=1.03–13.07). Kaplan–Meier analysis suggested significantly less time-dependent PJK development with tethering (p=0.027) at late follow-up (>3 months). Revision for PJK was required in 4 out of 34 NT patients (11.8%) versus 1/25 T patients (4%; p=0.289). Table 3 reports PJK rates, revision counts, and PJA change.

document_sections.heading: Predictors of PJK development
document_sections.content: In binary logistic regression, body mass index was a significant independent predictor of PJK (OR=1.23, CI95% 1.04–1.46; p=0.02). The reported model comparison with a null model was not significant, which the authors interpreted as good fit (p=0.06). The Cox regression model suggested lower PJK risk with tethering, but the association was not statistically significant (HR=0.33, 95%CI 0.08–1.31; p=0.11). Tables 4 and 5 present the multivariable logistic and Cox analyses, respectively.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: PJK burdens patients and is associated with worse health-related quality of life and dissatisfaction after surgery [9]. Additional interventions or revision surgery can lengthen recovery and add financial and emotional strain. Proposed preventive approaches include proximal tethers in several configurations [11, 12], prophylactic 2-level vertebroplasty [13, 14], transverse process hooks [15], flexible rods [16], multilevel stabilization screws [17], and sublaminar tapes [18]. The authors describe 2-level vertebroplasty, posterior tethers, and transverse process hooks as the most frequently studied approaches, with promising results [10]. In a finite element model, Bess and colleagues found that posterior tethers, compared with segmental pedicle screws and transverse process hooks, produced a more gradual transition in movement and stress across adjacent spinal segments [19]. Many earlier tether approaches targeted UIV+1 [6]; this study extended tethering to both UIV+1 and UIV+2. In the present cohort, univariable analysis found lower overall PJK rates with tethering. Tethers did not protect against PJK within the first 3 months but significantly reduced its incidence beyond 3 months. Rodriguez-Fontan et al., using Mersilene tape at UIV+1, observed greater sagittal Cobb-angle change in controls at 2 years than immediately after surgery or at 1.5 months, and concluded that protection becomes apparent within 2 years [20]. Buell et al. likewise found no significant tether-associated PJK reduction at 3 months but significantly lower rates at 6 months [11]. Among the risk factors examined in this study, body mass index (BMI) was the only significant independent predictor. Kaplan–Meier analysis indicated a greater probability of remaining PJK-free after surgery with tethering; Cox regression suggested lower cumulative PJK risk, although that result was not statistically significant. The authors consider the difference between odds-ratio findings and time-dependent analysis relevant to understanding when PJK develops. They did not assess correlations between radiographic PJK, symptoms, and clinical outcomes. Revision surgery instead served as an indirect indicator of symptoms or radiographic severity requiring intervention. Their overall surgical PJK incidence was 8.5%, compared with 6.7% in a meta-analysis by Luo et al. [21]. As in Buell et al. [22], revision rates were lower with tethers, but the difference was not statistically significant. Future research should examine how radiographic PJK relates to quality of life and symptom severity. For translaminar tether placement, the authors stress retaining enough bone around drill holes to prevent band cutout or pull-through: oversized or asymmetrically located holes may weaken the structure. Symmetrical tether placement and firm anchorage between UIV and UIV–1 are also important for balanced load distribution. Limitations include the retrospective design and potentially insufficient sample size for a complex outcome such as PJK, given only 25 tethered patients. The authors state that no other PJK-directed surgical techniques were used that might confound outcomes, and that baseline characteristics, surgical data, sagittal radiographic measurements, and correction extent were comparable between groups. They note that uncertainty about preventive strategies could make recruitment of larger cohorts difficult, while suggesting that this standardized technique may encourage larger prospective studies. Follow-up was also relatively short: average long-term follow-up ranged between 35–37 weeks, limiting assessment of longer-term tether outcomes. Cited literature indicates that most PJK occurs within the first 3 months [23, 24]. In a study with minimum 5-year follow-up, Yagi et al. found that 76% of PJK arose within the first 12 weeks and that no patient developed PJK after 5 years; the mean PJA increase at 12 weeks represented 53% of the increase at final follow-up [24]. In the present study, 55% of patients who developed PJK did so within the first 3 months. The authors suggest that early PJK may be influenced by low bone quality, reduced muscle mass, and alignment-related factors. Correction targets may not suit every patient and may produce under- or over-correction. Such pre-existing factors might explain the absence of an early tethering benefit, whereas later PJK may reflect progressively accumulated proximal mechanical loading that the tether construct could help moderate. Because PJK has multiple contributing factors, further studies are needed to distinguish early from late mechanisms and support a more individualized approach.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: In patients undergoing thoraco-lumbar deformity correction, polyester tethers at UIV+1 and UIV+2 significantly lowered overall PJK incidence and increased the probability of remaining PJK-free after surgery. Whether translaminar tethering affects revision surgery for PJK remains uncertain. Prospective long-term observation is needed to clarify PJK progression and its effects on clinical outcomes.
